slot.brief: A ball strikes a smooth surface obliquely and rebounds; use momentum components along and normal to the wall with a given coefficient of restitution to find rebound speed and angle.

stem: A small ball strikes a smooth vertical wall with a speed of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the normal. If the coefficient of restitution is $e = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, the speed of the ball and its angle of rebound with the normal are, respectively:

verdicts.working: Normal component = 20cos30° = 10√3 m/s; after impact = e·10√3 = 10 m/s. Tangential component unchanged (smooth wall) = 20sin30° = 10 m/s. Rebound speed = √(10²+10²) = 10√2 m/s; angle with normal = arctan(10/10) = 45°.

working:
1. Resolve the velocity before impact into components parallel and perpendicular to the wall:
$$\text{Parallel (tangential): } u_\parallel = u \sin 30^\circ = 20 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$\text{Perpendicular (normal): } u_\perp = u \cos 30^\circ = 20 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

2. Since the wall is smooth, there is no impulse parallel to the wall, so the tangential component remains unchanged:
$$v_\parallel = u_\parallel = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

3. The normal component is reduced by the coefficient of restitution $e$:
$$v_\perp = e u_\perp = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times 10\sqrt{3} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

4. Rebound speed:
$$v = \sqrt{v_\parallel^2 + v_\perp^2} = \sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = 10\sqrt{2}\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

5. Angle with the normal ($\theta'$):
$$\tan\theta' = \dfrac{v_\parallel}{v_\perp} = \dfrac{10}{10} = 1 \implies \theta' = 45^\circ$$

Thus, the speed is $10\sqrt{2}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the angle is $45^\circ$.

Independent check: Normal component = 20cos30° = 10√3 m/s; after impact = e·10√3 = 10 m/s. Tangential component unchanged (smooth wall) = 20sin30° = 10 m/s. Rebound speed = √(10²+10²) = 10√2 m/s; angle with normal = arctan(10/10) = 45°.

draft.distractor_notes:
Option A: Correctly calculates the rebound speed but incorrectly assumes the law of reflection holds (angle of rebound equals angle of incidence, 30°).
Option C: Treats the collision as perfectly elastic (e = 1), keeping the initial speed of 20 m/s and angle of 30° unchanged.
Option D: Correctly determines the rebound angle of 45° but neglects kinetic energy loss, retaining the initial speed of 20 m/s.
